## Proof

**Step 1: Identify the Lie algebra structure.**

The given Lie algebra is 3-dimensional:
$$\mathfrak{g} = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}0 &-a&u\\ a &0&v\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}; a,u,v\in\mathbb{R}\right\}$$

Choose the basis:
- $X_1 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &-1&0\\ 1 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$ (set $a=1, u=v=0$)
- $X_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &0&1\\ 0 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$ (set $u=1$)
- $X_3 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &0&0\\ 0 &0&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}$ (set $v=1$)

**Step 2: Compute the commutators.**

$[X_1, X_2] = X_1X_2 - X_2X_1$. Computing:
$$X_1X_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &-1&0\\ 1 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 &0&1\\ 0 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = X_3$$
$$X_2X_1 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &0&1\\ 0 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 &-1&0\\ 1 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = 0$$
So $[X_1, X_2] = X_3$.

$[X_1, X_3] = X_1X_3 - X_3X_1$. Computing:
$$X_1X_3 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &-1&0\\ 1 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 &0&0\\ 0 &0&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}0&0&-1\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = -X_2$$
$$X_3X_1 = \begin{bmatrix}0 &0&0\\ 0 &0&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 &-1&0\\ 1 &0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} = 0$$
So $[X_1, X_3] = -X_2$.

$[X_2, X_3] = 0$ since both $X_2, X_3$ are strictly upper-triangular nilpotent matrices whose products vanish.

**Step 3: Interpret the structure.**

The commutator relations are:
$$[X_1, X_2] = X_3,\quad [X_1, X_3] = -X_2,\quad [X_2, X_3] = 0.$$

The subalgebra $\mathfrak{so}(2) = \mathrm{span}\{X_1\}$ acts on the abelian ideal $\mathfrak{n} = \mathrm{span}\{X_2, X_3\} \cong \mathbb{R}^2$ by rotation: $\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$ acts on $\mathfrak{n}$ as the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ (in the basis $\{X_2, X_3\}$, since $[X_1, X_2]=X_3$ and $[X_1,X_3]=-X_2$). This is precisely the infinitesimal rotation action of $\mathfrak{so}(2)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Thus $\mathfrak{g} \cong \mathfrak{so}(2) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^2$, a semidirect product Lie algebra.

**Step 4: Identify the Lie group.**

The Lie group whose Lie algebra is $\mathfrak{so}(2) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^2$ is the **special Euclidean group of the plane**:
$$G = SE(2) = SO(2) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^2,$$
the group of orientation-preserving rigid motions (isometries) of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Concretely, $SE(2)$ is realized as the matrix group:
$$SE(2) = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta & x\\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta & y\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix};\ \theta\in\mathbb{R},\ x,y\in\mathbb{R}\right\}.$$

**Verification:** The Lie algebra of this matrix group is obtained by differentiating at the identity ($\theta=0, x=y=0$). Setting $\theta = at$, $x = ut$, $y = vt$ and differentiating at $t=0$ yields exactly:
$$\mathfrak{se}(2) = \left\{\begin{bmatrix}0 &-a&u\\ a &0&v\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix};\ a,u,v\in\mathbb{R}\right\},$$
which matches the given $Lie(G)$ exactly. The group operation is the semidirect product $(R_1, t_1)\cdot(R_2, t_2) = (R_1 R_2,\ R_1 t_2 + t_1)$, reflecting that $SO(2)$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by rotation.

**Conclusion:** The Lie group $G$ is $SE(2) = SO(2) \ltimes \mathbb{R}^2$, the special Euclidean group of the plane — the group of orientation-preserving rigid motions of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
